titre: The handwriting that, according to Bertillon, forged itself
accroche: December 1894: Bertillon presents to the court-martial diagrams proving, he says, that Dreyfus had disguised his own handwriting.
contenu_vulgarise:
## Wastebasket scraps become evidence

In late September 1894, a cleaning woman employed by the French secret services, emptying the wastebaskets of the German embassy in Paris, hands the officers of the 2nd Bureau the torn pieces of an unsigned letter. Pieced back together, it promises the German attaché the delivery of French military plans: this is the “bordereau.” On October 15, Captain Alfred Dreyfus, a General Staff officer of Alsatian origin, is summoned to the War Ministry and asked to write from dictation, without being told why. Five handwriting experts are then consulted. Two of them, including Alfred Gobert, the Banque de France's usual expert, judge that the handwriting of the bordereau cannot be attributed to Dreyfus. Three others (Teyssonnières, Charavay with a reservation, and Alphonse Bertillon) conclude the opposite.

## A theory built to explain what does not fit

Bertillon is not a graphologist: he runs the judicial identity service of the Paris police prefecture and built his reputation on measuring the human body, not on handwriting. Faced with visible differences between the bordereau and Dreyfus's handwriting, he does not conclude innocence: he builds an explanation that turns the difference into proof. His thesis, known as “self-forgery,” claims that Dreyfus knowingly disguised his own hand by tracing that of his brother Mathieu: the word “intérêt,” found identical in a letter from the latter, serves him as a template. Using a ruler and a five-centime coin as measuring instruments, Bertillon overlays words, cuts out grids, and claims to recognize in the document at least three different handwritings, all from one hand expert in concealment. On December 21, 1894, he sets out this demonstration to the Paris court-martial, behind closed doors, with diagrams. The reasoning does not convince all the judges, but it carries weight: on December 22, they unanimously sentence Dreyfus to military degradation and deportation for life.

## It took mathematicians to dismantle a system that claimed to be mathematical

The case is retried twice. The French Court of Cassation quashes a first judgment on June 3, 1899, and sends Dreyfus before the Rennes court-martial, which declares him guilty a second time, “with extenuating circumstances” for a crime of treason, on September 9, 1899, before he is pardoned ten days later, without being exonerated. It is not a graphologist who ends Bertillon's thesis, but three members of the Academy of Sciences: Paul Appell, Gaston Darboux and Henri Poincaré, commissioned by the Court of Cassation to examine his probability calculations. Their report, delivered on August 2, 1904, concludes that the method rests on no scientific basis: the matches retained had been chosen after the fact, and the calculation of probabilities, applied to an approximate photographic reconstruction of the torn bordereau, proved nothing of what it claimed to demonstrate. On July 12, 1906, the Court of Cassation, with all chambers sitting together, quashes the Rennes judgment without remand and declares Dreyfus innocent.

What strikes us, with more than a century's hindsight, is not only Bertillon's error: it is that authority from an entirely different discipline, mathematics, had to be borrowed to contradict a demonstration that itself presented itself as rigorously scientific. A diagram, a ruler and a vocabulary of measurement had been enough, in 1894, to pass off an intuition as proof, and to turn the doubt of two experts out of five into a detail that could go unheard.

repere.texte: Of the five handwriting experts consulted in 1894, two (Gobert and Pelletier) judge that the bordereau cannot be attributed to Dreyfus; three (Teyssonnières, Charavay and Bertillon) conclude the opposite. It is this latter view, carried by Bertillon's “self-forgery” thesis, that prevails at the court-martial.
repere.source: Jean Jaurès, “Les Preuves — Le Bordereau et les premiers experts,” La Petite République, 1898

carte.punch: The expert saw in every difference in handwriting the proof of a disguise, not of a mistake
carte.idee: In 1894, Alphonse Bertillon claims that the differences between the bordereau and Dreyfus's handwriting prove he disguised his hand. His “self-forgery” thesis, judged pseudo-scientific by three mathematicians in 1904, weighs on his conviction; Dreyfus is exonerated in 1906.

quiz.question: Why is Bertillon's “self-forgery” thesis now judged pseudo-scientific?
choix: Because no other expert consulted in 1894 had questioned the attribution of the bordereau to Dreyfus
Because it interprets after the fact selected resemblances with an unsuitable probability calculation
Because Bertillon had never compared the bordereau with a text actually written by Dreyfus
Because the bordereau itself turned out to be a document fabricated after the fact by the French army
quiz.explication: The 1904 report (Appell, Darboux, Poincaré) shows that the matches Bertillon retained had been chosen after the fact and that his probability calculation did not apply to this type of comparison. Two of the five experts of 1894 already doubted the attribution; Dreyfus had indeed written from dictation for the comparison; and it is another document, the “Henry forgery,” not the bordereau, that was fabricated later in the affair.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How many handwriting experts were consulted in 1894, and how many of them rejected the attribution of the bordereau to Dreyfus?
choix: Three experts, all in favor of attributing it to Dreyfus
Five experts, two of whom rejected the attribution to Dreyfus
Five experts, unanimous in attributing the bordereau to Dreyfus
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Of the five experts consulted, Gobert (the Banque de France's usual expert) and Pelletier judge that the handwriting cannot be attributed to Dreyfus; the other three, including Bertillon, conclude the opposite.

quiz_supplementaire.question: On what had Bertillon built his reputation before intervening in the Dreyfus affair?
choix: On his post as a law professor at the Sorbonne
On decades of expertise in forensic graphology
On anthropometric measurement of the human body
On running the police prefecture's chemistry laboratory
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text states that Bertillon is not a graphologist: he runs the judicial identity service and built his reputation on measuring the human body, not on handwriting expertise.

quiz_supplementaire.question: On what element does Bertillon rely to claim that Dreyfus imitated his own brother's handwriting?
choix: A letter signed jointly by the two brothers in 1893
The testimony of a Banque de France employee
A chemical comparison of the ink used by the two brothers
A word, “intérêt,” found identical in a letter from his brother Mathieu
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Bertillon uses the word “intérêt,” found identical in a letter from Mathieu Dreyfus, as a template to argue that Dreyfus traced his hand on his brother's.
